title: The Harvesters
credit: Rogers Fund, 1919. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Contemporaries nicknamed him “Peasant Bruegel.” Karel van Mander later wrote that he and a friend would put on country clothes, turn up at village weddings and kermises with a gift, and sketch the room as if they belonged there.

title: Madame X (Madame Pierre Gautreau)
credit: Arthur Hoppock Hearn Fund, 1916. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Sargent was a fixture of the same drawing rooms he painted: an American raised on the European circuit who often sat down at the piano between sittings. After the Madame X scandal he rebuilt his career in London, then in 1907 tried to swear off society portraits altogether—“No more paughtraits.”

title: The Death of Socrates
credit: Catharine Lorillard Wolfe Collection, Wolfe Fund, 1931. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: David did not stay in the studio. As a Jacobin deputy he voted for the death of Louis XVI, later became Napoleon’s official image-maker, and after the monarchy returned died in exile in Brussels.

title: The Dance Class
credit: Bequest of Mrs. Harry Payne Bingham, 1986. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Degas grew up in a banking family, never married, and was famous among friends for a sharp tongue. In later life his eyesight failed so badly that he leaned on pastels and sculpture—still watching from the wings rather than taking center stage.

title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
credit: Purchase, The Annenberg Foundation Gift, 1993. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Van Gogh’s real autobiography is the hundreds of letters he sent his brother Theo, a Paris art dealer who floated him with a monthly allowance. From the asylum at Saint-Rémy he wrote that the cypresses were “beautiful as an Egyptian obelisk,” then painted this field to prove it.

title: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
credit: Marquand Collection, Gift of Henry G. Marquand, 1889. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Vermeer died suddenly in 1675, ruined after the 1672 collapse of the Dutch art market. His widow Catharina had to petition for insolvency and surrender paintings to settle debts—the quiet Delft interiors were the opposite of that last year.

title: Cypresses
credit: Rogers Fund, 1949. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: In May 1889 van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum at Saint-Rémy. He wrote Theo that the cypresses were “always occupying my thoughts,” and between crises he worked on the hospital grounds as if the trees were sitters who would not keep still.

title: Irises
credit: Gift of Adele R. Levy, 1958. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: For most of Vincent’s working life, Theo sent money almost every month; canvases traveled north in return, like illustrated letters. He painted these irises in May 1890, the week before he left the Saint-Rémy asylum for Auvers.

title: Boating
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Manet’s father was a senior official at the Ministry of Justice and expected his son to study law. Édouard became the reluctant elder of Impressionism instead—friends with Monet, yet he refused their independent shows and kept courting the official Salon.

title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
credit: Purchase, special contributions and funds given or bequeathed by friends of the Museum, 1961. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: In 1656 Rembrandt declared insolvency, and the contents of his Amsterdam house—prints, studio props, and a cabinet of curiosities—went to auction. He spent his later years on the Rozengracht, still painting, no longer a rich collector of other people’s treasures.

title: The Horse Fair
credit: Gift of Cornelius Vanderbilt, 1887. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: To sketch at the Paris horse market and slaughterhouses, Bonheur secured an official police permit to wear trousers—a permission French women then had to renew in writing. In 1865 Empress Eugénie made her the first woman artist awarded the Legion of Honour, remarking that “genius has no sex.”

title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
credit: Gift of John Stewart Kennedy, 1897. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)
description: Leutze was a German-American: born in Württemberg, raised in Philadelphia, then back in Düsseldorf when he painted this ice using the Rhine as a stand-in. He meant the picture as a pep talk for Europe’s 1848 liberal revolutions as much as for American schoolrooms.
